opus-5.5.text:
I think both ecosystems are willing to bet big, but they bet in different ways.

In Silicon Valley, the funding tends to follow a very particular thesis: that scaling works. People watched what happened with large language models, where putting more data and more compute into a fairly general architecture produced capabilities nobody had explicitly engineered. So many investors and large labs are now willing to write very large checks on the hypothesis that the same thing will happen for robotics, that a sufficiently large foundation model trained on enough embodied data will eventually generalize across tasks, environments, and even robot bodies. That is a long-horizon bet. You may not see a product for years, and the capital in the Valley is fairly comfortable with that, at least for now, because the upside if it works is enormous.

In China, my impression is that the appetite is just as strong, but it is more grounded in hardware and deployment. China has an incredible manufacturing and supply-chain advantage. You can iterate on a humanoid or a robot arm much faster and much more cheaply, and there are many companies shipping real robots into real settings. So the funding often goes toward getting physical systems out the door, finding near-term applications, and learning from that. There is also significant support at the policy and local government level for embodied intelligence as a strategic industry, which changes the risk calculus for investors.

Neither approach is strictly better. The fundamental bottleneck in robotics is data. Unlike text, there is no internet of robot experience to scrape. The Silicon Valley approach tries to solve that through better models, simulation, cross-embodiment learning, and leveraging vision-language pretraining. The China approach may solve it by simply having many more robots in the world collecting real data. In the long run, I suspect the winners will need both: strong foundation models and a hardware flywheel that keeps feeding them real-world experience.

One thing I would caution about on both sides is hype. Robotics has gone through several cycles where expectations ran ahead of reality. The progress in the last two or three years is real and exciting, but general-purpose robots that work reliably in homes are still a hard problem. The funders who will do well are the ones patient enough to stay through the slower phases, not just the demo phase.

r001.rationale: The response says Chinese funding often favors deployment and near-term applications, but does not clearly say that access to funding depends on demonstrating short-term progress.

r002.rationale: It discusses robotics data as a bottleneck but does not mention a few hundred hours of data or say that amount is insufficient to validate a scaling law.

r003.rationale: It does not describe an initial investment being too small to produce results needed to secure further investment.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Musk or attribute Silicon Valley investors’ willingness to fund ambitious projects to his successes.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer this directly as the guest.

I think the difference is less about courage and more about where each side believes the leverage is.

In Silicon Valley, the capital is comfortable with a long, abstract bet. Investors there have watched large language models go from a research curiosity to a multi-hundred-billion-dollar industry in a few years, so when someone says "we're going to do the same thing for the physical world," they already have the pattern in their heads. They'll fund a team that has no product, no revenue, maybe not even a working robot, if the team can tell a convincing story about data, scaling, and a foundation model for action. The risk appetite is high, but so is the patience. People accept that the first few years might produce nothing but demos.

In China, the appetite for robotics is enormous, arguably bigger, but it tends to attach itself to something tangible. There's a very deep manufacturing base, the supply chain for motors, actuators, sensors is right there, and the cost of building hardware is a fraction of what it is in the US. So the natural instinct is: build the body, ship something, find a real scenario, and let the intelligence catch up. The funding often comes with an expectation that you'll be in a factory or a logistics warehouse relatively quickly. That makes the ecosystem incredibly fast at iterating on hardware, and sometimes less willing to spend three years on a model whose only output is a research paper.

I'd put it this way: Silicon Valley is more willing to fund the brain before the body exists. China is more willing to fund the body before the brain exists. Each side has a blind spot. The Valley can underestimate how hard and how slow hardware really is, how much reliability and cost matter once you leave the lab. China can underestimate how much the breakthrough in general-purpose robotics is fundamentally a learning problem, where the expensive, unglamorous part is collecting diverse data and training at scale.

What's interesting to me is that the gap is narrowing. The success of large models globally has made Chinese investors more open to the "foundation model for robots" thesis, and some of the most ambitious embodied AI teams in China now get funded at valuations that would have been unthinkable a few years ago. At the same time, US companies are realizing they cannot ignore the hardware side and are either building their own or quietly sourcing from China.

So if you ask where I'd want to be, honestly the ideal company has both instincts in it. You want the willingness to make the long, scary bet on learning, and you want the discipline of someone who has actually had to ship a robot that works at eight in the morning on a factory floor. Neither ecosystem has fully combined those yet, and I think whoever does will define the field.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention robotics data hours or whether that amount can validate a scaling law.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate willingness to invest from willingness to stay invested. Large-model robotics requires more than training a model. You need hardware, data collection, real-world testing, and many rounds of iteration. The question is whether investors will keep supporting that process when progress is uneven.

My impression is that Silicon Valley is more comfortable funding a very ambitious technical thesis before the business model is clear. That gives teams room to pursue something with a long horizon, although it also creates pressure to tell a bigger story than the technology can yet support.

In China, the conversation tends to move more quickly toward applications: Where will the robot work? What does it cost? What value does it create? And the manufacturing ecosystem can make it easier to turn an idea into hardware and iterate. That’s a substantial advantage, though demanding commercial results too early can constrain longer-term research.

So I wouldn’t describe it as one side being ambitious and the other not. They have different strengths. What robotics needs is a combination: the patience to fund a difficult technical leap and the discipline to test whether it actually works in the real world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is how investors think about risk and the time horizon. Training a large model for robotics takes substantial capital, and the path from a compelling demonstration to a reliable commercial product can be long. You’re dealing with hardware, data collection, safety, and deployment—not just model training.

In Silicon Valley, there tends to be more willingness to fund a very ambitious technical vision before the business model is fully clear. In China, investors often put more emphasis on applications, commercialization, and how quickly a company can generate revenue. But I wouldn’t make that an absolute distinction; you can find patient investors and short-term thinking in both places.

China also has a strong manufacturing ecosystem, which can make building and iterating on robots easier. So willingness to fund the research is only one part of the picture. The bigger question is whether you can bring together patient capital, strong researchers, and the ability to turn those models into robots that work reliably in the real world.
